nt: Here, **Zion** represents the temple and the community of God’s people who worshiped there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [our homeland]

nt: The psalmist refers to **willows** that are a kind of tree. If your readers would not be familiar with what willows are, you could use the name of another kind of tree that was common in that part of the world that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [On the trees in Babylon]

x.Darby: For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that made us wail [required] mirth, [saying,] Sing us [one] of the songs of Zion.

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and our tormentors requested of us joy]

x.ASV: How shall we sing Jehovah’s song In a foreign land?
x.Darby: How should we sing a song of Jehovah's upon a foreign soil?
x.KJV: How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a strange land?
x.YLT: How do we sing the song of Jehovah, On the land of a stranger?

nt: אֵ֗יךְ נָשִׁ֥יר אֶת־שִׁיר־יְהוָ֑ה עַ֝֗ל אַדְמַ֥ת נֵכָֽר

The psalmist is using the question form to emphasize that the people of Israel were not able to sing the song of Yahweh while in exile. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We cannot sing the song of Yahweh on the land of foreignness!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **foreignness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in a land that is not our own]

x.ASV: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, Let my right hand forget her skill.
x.Darby: If I forget thee, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget [its skill];
x.KJV: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning.
x.YLT: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, my right hand forgetteth!

nt: The psalmist is presenting a possible condition and its consequence. He says that if he forgets Jerusalem, then his right hand should no longer be able to play the harp. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [If I forget you, Jerusalem, then let my right hand forget]
Here the psalmist shifts from speaking about the community as “we” in the previous verses to speaking as an individual using the pronoun **I**. He is making a personal vow.

The psalmist is using **let my right hand forget** as a common expression of the culture to mean that his hand would lose its ability to play a musical instrument. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let my right hand lose its skill] or [let my right hand wither]

The psalmist is saying what he wants to happen if he breaks his vow. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that my right hand would forget] or [may my right hand forget]

x.ASV: Let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth, If I remember thee not; If I prefer not Jerusalem Above my chief joy.
x.Darby: If I do not remember thee, let my tongue cleave to my palate: if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy.
x.KJV: If I do not remember thee, let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth; if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy.
x.YLT: My tongue doth cleave to my palate, If I do not remember thee, If I do not exalt Jerusalem above my chief joy.

nt: תִּדְבַּ֥ק־לְשׁוֹנִ֨⁠י ׀ לְ⁠חִכִּ⁠י֮ אִם־לֹ֪א אֶ֫זְכְּרֵ֥⁠כִי אִם־לֹ֣א אַ֭עֲלֶה אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֑ם עַ֝֗ל רֹ֣אשׁ שִׂמְחָתִֽ⁠י

The psalmist is presenting the consequence first and then the condition. It may be helpful to reorder this sentence so that the conditional statement is first. Alternate translation: [If I fail to remember you, if I do not cause Jerusalem to go up above the head of my joy, then let me tongue cling to my palate]

The psalmist is using **tongue cling to my palate** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he would be unable to speak or sing. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let me be unable to sing] or [Let my mouth be silenced]
אִם־לֹ֣א אַ֭עֲלֶה אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֑ם עַ֝֗ל רֹ֣אשׁ שִׂמְחָתִֽ⁠י

The psalmist is using **go up above the head** as a common expression of the culture to mean to the “highest point” or “greatest extent.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [if I do not cause Jerusalem to give me more joy than anything else]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what makes me rejoice]

x.ASV: Remember, O Jehovah, against the children of Edom The day of Jerusalem; Who said, Rase it, rase it, Even to the foundation thereof.
x.Darby: Remember, O Jehovah, against the sons of Edom, the day of Jerusalem; who said, Lay [it] bare, Lay [it] bare, down to its foundation!
x.KJV: Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem; who said, Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof.
x.YLT: Remember, Jehovah, for the sons of Edom, The day of Jerusalem, Those saying, `Rase, rase to its foundation!'

nt: The psalmist is speaking as if the people of the tribe of Esau were actually the **sons** of Edom, another name for Esau. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Esau] or [the people of Edom]

The psalmist is using **the day of Jerusalem** as a common expression of the culture to mean the time when Jerusalem was destroyed. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what happened to Jerusalem] or [the destruction of Jerusalem]

The psalmist is using repetition of the phrase **lay bare** for poetic effect. You may want to reproduce this effect if poetry in your language does this. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Completely demolish]
The pronoun **her** refers to Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in Jerusalem]

t: that/ is about to be destroyed

x.ASV: O daughter of Babylon, that art to be destroyed, Happy shall he be, that rewardeth thee As thou hast served us.
x.Darby: Daughter of Babylon, who art to be laid waste, happy he that rendereth unto thee that which thou hast meted out to us.
x.KJV: O daughter of Babylon, who art to be destroyed; happy shall he be, that rewardeth thee as thou hast served us.
x.YLT: O daughter of Babylon, O destroyed one, O the happiness of him who repayeth to thee thy deed, That thou hast done to us.

nt: The psalmist is speaking of **Babylon** as if it were a woman by calling it **Daughter**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Babylon] or [The city of Babylon]

The psalmist is speaking to **Babylon** as if the city could hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the judgment that Babylon deserves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Babylon. Alternate translation: [As for Babylon]

The phrase **the devastated one** is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. You may want to follow an alternative reading from some ancient Greek and Aramaic translations. The UST follows that reading. Alternate translation: [you destroyer]

The psalmist is using an exclamation to express a strong desire for justice against Babylon. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [how happy is]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **repayment**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in order to repay you for all you did to us]
